query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal shock treatment applied to the HEA will trigger the in situ formation of a nanostructured, self-healing lubricious oxide layer (e.g., a ZrTiO4‐like phase) on its surface, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a wide service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated high-entropy alloy with a conventional microstructure lacking a dedicated lubricious phase.
generation.intervention: A single-step controlled thermal shock (or short annealing) treatment—for example, rapidly heating the alloy to about 800°C for 1 hour—to modify only the surface.
generation.conditions: Effective under wide temperature conditions ranging from room temperature to several hundred degrees Celsius, mimicking service environments in self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, nanostructured lubricious oxide layer, likely a ZrTiO4-like phase, that is both self-healing and thermally stable.
generation.mechanism: The thermal shock initiates rapid surface oxidation and phase transformation that yields a protective oxide layer. This layer reduces shear strength at the friction interface and can self-heal under cyclic sliding, thereby lowering both friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated HEA is expected to show a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate, compared to the untreated alloy, under the full range of operating temperatures.
generation.baseline: The tribological performance (friction coefficient and wear rate) of the untreated HEA under similar temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected as long as the thermal treatment induces a complete and stable lubricious oxide layer; if the treatment is insufficient to form the oxide or if the oxide layer delaminates/degrades at extreme temperatures, the benefit may not be realized.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thermal profile (temperature, time, and cooling rate) required for robust oxide formation is not precisely known. Additionally, the magnitude of improvement may vary with specific alloy composition and processing precision.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens. Subject one set to the controlled thermal shock treatment (e.g., 800°C for 1 hour) while leaving the other set untreated. Then, perform tribological tests over a broad temperature range (from room temperature to ~500°C) using identical sliding conditions.
measurements: Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to confirm the formation and stability of the lubricious oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not consistently show a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate compared to untreated samples across the tested temperature range, or if surface characterization fails to confirm formation of a stable oxide layer, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Inspired by the high-entropy effects, we replace minor alloying elements in nickel-based alloys with multicomponent alloying elements, which not only deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in the system but also enhance the ability of the system to generate glaze layers. This cooperative heterostructure can trigger gradient recrystallized tribo-layer through plastic deformation co-mediated by dislocation, SFs, and deformation twins (DT) during sliding at RT, thus accommodating elastic–plastic deformation and virtually eliminating wear. The intrinsic composition undulations can stabilize the friction interface and act twofold, not only by circumventing strain localization in the NC tribo-layer but also by densifying the glaze layer. We realize the above strategy in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 (at.%) CCA and reveal the origin of the nanohierarchical architecture by comparing it with its counterpart Ni75(AlNbTiV)25 CCA with lower alloying concentration (hereinafter named NiX and Ni3X, respectively). The wear mechanisms addressed in this work provide guidance for the fabrication of ultra-wear-resistant alloys by exploiting the multicomponent heterostructure

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

frame.system: A high‐entropy alloy (HEA) used in self‐lubricating moving components, currently in its untreated state with conventional microstructure and without a dedicated lubricious phase.
frame.goal: Achieve a simultaneous reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate over a broad range of service temperatures.
frame.limitation: The untreated HEA exhibits high friction and accelerated wear under variable temperature conditions; previous multi-step or surface-only modifications have not delivered consistent tribological improvements across the entire temperature range.
constraints: must improve both friction and wear relative to the untreated alloy
should be effective over a broad (wide) temperature range
mechanistic explanation, quantitative performance prediction, and experimental falsifiability are required
frame.regime: Performance must be maintained from ambient conditions to elevated temperatures (e.g., room temperature up to several hundred degrees Celsius) typical of service conditions in moving components.
prior_attempts: Use of conventional surface coatings or multi-stage treatments that improve friction at one temperature extreme but tend to degrade at the other end of the temperature spectrum.
Attempts to incorporate separate solid lubricants which often fail to self-adapt over the wide temperature variation.

decision.trend: Early studies improved wear resistance and friction in HEAs by tuning bulk microstructures and inducing dual-phase architectures (e.g., inverse Hall‐Petch effects and nanoprecipitates) to enhance hardness and reduce wear. More recent work has shifted toward engineering near-surface adaptations that can form adaptive, self-healing tribo-films; for example, nanohierarchical architectures with composition undulation (PMC10241162) and thermal treatments that trigger in situ formation of protective oxide layers (PMC10456374) have demonstrated extreme wear resistance over broad temperatures. In parallel, 2D HEA nanoflakes with tribocatalytic activity (PMC12019924) have shown that engineered surfaces, rather than added solid lubricants, can achieve ultra-low friction even under high contact pressures.
decision.unsolved: Despite these advances, there remains no single-step intervention in untreated HEAs that reliably forms a robust and adaptive lubricious interface effective over a wide service-temperature range. Previous strategies either require multi-step processing, extrinsic coatings, or introduce additional phases that may fail to perform uniformly across the temperature spectrum.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled thermal shock (or short annealing) treatment designed to trigger the in situ formation of a nanostructured, self-healing lubricious oxide (e.g., a ZrTiO4-like phase) on the HEA surface
decision.why: This next step capitalizes on the trend toward adaptive tribo-interface formation observed in recent studies and directly addresses the gap by using a single processing intervention that modifies only the surface. Such a treatment is expected to lower both the friction coefficient and wear rate by generating a stable, temperature-resilient lubricious layer, thereby meeting the design goal without relying on multi-step or external coating processes.
